newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Landmines maim long after wars end.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Landmines maim long after wars end.

text.p: By Geert De Clercq,
Kamel Saadi, 14, was enjoying a barbecue with his family in the hills of north-west Jordan. Suddenly, there was an enormous noise.
"I was thrown in the air, there was a smell of barbecue, but not to eat. It was my own smell," Saadi told Reuters in an interview at the Brussels Conference on a Global Ban on Antipersonnel Mines.
"I tried to run, but I couldn't. There was blood all over the grass. Then I saw that my foot was blown off," he said.
It was eight hours before he got to a hospital, where his foot was amputated. But pain persisted, and six years later, in 1985, doctors had to cut of his leg 20 centimetres below the knee.

Saadi, now 33, is married and has a child, works in his father's book shop and has studied prosthetics. He walks virtually without a limp on the artificial leg he made himself and fits limbs to others in his spare time.
"I am one of the lucky ones," he said. "You should see the face of a mine victim when he walks again for the first time - that mixture of fear and joy, just like a baby."
Every year, the 110 million or so landmines left all over the world kill 26,000 people, one every 20 minutes.
Many landmine victims never make it to a hospital, bleeding to death in remote areas.
Thirteen survivors, including a 12-year old Bosnian boy, came to the Brussels Conference to bear witness to their plight.
"We came here to testify with our bodies, so that you can see what mines have done to us," Cambodian Tun Channereth, who lost both legs from the knee down, said in speech to delegates.
LANDMINE BAN CAMPAIGN SCORES FIRST VICTORY

The campaign to ban landmines has started fairly recently. In 1991-92 a handful of non-governmental organisations pooled their efforts to form the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, which now represents more than 1,000 groups.
A first landmark in the drive for a global ban on anti-personnel mines was when Belgium unilaterally pledged to stop using land mines in March 1995.

A year later, the Canadian government put its weight behind a campaign for a global ban on the production, use, stockpiling and trade in mines. At a conference in Ottawa last October, Canada launched a drive to get countries to sign an anti-mine treaty in Ottawa in December 1997.
That effort, known as the Ottawa Process, scored a landmark victory at the Brussels halfway conference, where 95 states pledged to sign the Ottawa treaty.
Meanwhile, separate talks on land mines continue at the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.

The Geneva talks, which require unanimity for a deal, are not expected to produce a ban for years to come but they are the only forum which brings in states that do not partake in the Ottawa talks, notably the United States and China.
LAND MINE TERROR TO LAST FOR DECADES
Even if all countries in the world were to stop using mines now, the 110 million or so mines lurking in the soil in some 60 countries are set to menace populations for decades to come.
As war injuries go, land mines wounds are the worst there are, Canadian war surgeon Chris Paul Giannou told Reuters.
Those who step on a blast mine usually loose a foot or a leg and suffer severe injuries to the other leg, genitalia and arms.
As the blast tears through tissue, it burns flesh and drives soil, grass, gravel, mine fragments, clothing and bone deep into the leg and other parts of the body.
Besides posing a medical nightmare, mines also wreak havoc on the economies of mine-infested countries, as they render large tracts of land useless for agriculture.
"It is not the quantity of mines that matters. A few mines can depopulate an entire area," said Alex Vines, author of a study on mines for Human Rights Watch.
ONE MINE CLEARER KILLED FOR EVERY 5,000 MINES REMOVED
The problems facing the groups who clear mines are daunting.
Mines comes in a bewildering number of shapes, from tiny button-mines, scattered from planes by the thousands, to trip-wire mines, designed to jump up and explode in the air.
A particularly nasty brand is the small Russian butterfly mine. A child may pick it up, thinking it a toy, until it explodes.
Anti-personnel mines are not designed to kill. Their aim is to maim, so that other soldiers will be have to care for the victim.
While a mine costs only between $3 to $30 to produce, clearing it costs an average of $1,000.
"It takes a 30-man team of professional deminers a full day to clear a band of 10 metres wide and 100 metres long," Belgian army mine clearance unit sergeant David Smith told Reuters.
The Red Cross estimates that for every 5,000 mines cleared, one mine-clearing expert is killed and two are injured.
